task: Extract the last word from text
intro: Excel has no built-in function that returns only the last word of a text string, but you can combine TRIM, RIGHT, SUBSTITUTE and REPT — or use TEXTAFTER in Microsoft 365.

steps.heading: Modern Excel (Microsoft 365): TEXTAFTER
steps.body: Use =TEXTAFTER(A1," ",-1) to return everything after the last space — i.e. the last word.

steps.heading: Older versions: combine functions
steps.body: Use =TRIM(RIGHT(SUBSTITUTE(A1," ",REPT(" ",100)),100)). SUBSTITUTE replaces each space with 100 spaces, RIGHT grabs the last 100 characters, and TRIM removes the padding.

formulas.explanation: Returns the text after the last space (Microsoft 365 only).
Works in every Excel version; pads spaces then takes the rightmost characters.

task: Extract the first word from text
intro: Pulling the first word out of a cell is a LEFT + FIND combination in every Excel version — or a one-argument TEXTBEFORE call in Microsoft 365.

steps.heading: Modern Excel (Microsoft 365): TEXTBEFORE
steps.body: Use =TEXTBEFORE(A1," ") to return everything before the first space.

steps.heading: All versions: LEFT + FIND
steps.body: Use =LEFT(A1,FIND(" ",A1)-1). FIND locates the space; subtracting 1 excludes it.

steps.heading: Handle single-word cells
steps.body: FIND errors when there is no space. Wrap in IFERROR to return the whole cell: =IFERROR(LEFT(A1,FIND(" ",A1)-1),A1).

formulas.explanation: Microsoft 365 only — text before the first space.
Works everywhere; falls back to the full cell when no space exists.

intro: Excel ships a one-click Remove Duplicates tool on the Data tab — but a COUNTIF helper column is the better route when you want to review dupes before deleting them.

steps.heading: Quick way: Data → Remove Duplicates
steps.body: Select the range, go to Data → Remove Duplicates, pick the columns that define 'same', and click OK. Excel reports how many duplicates were removed.

steps.heading: Review first: COUNTIF flag
steps.body: Add a helper column with =COUNTIF($A$2:$A$100,A2)>1. TRUE rows are duplicates — filter on it, inspect, then delete.

steps.heading: Modern Excel: UNIQUE
steps.body: In Microsoft 365, =UNIQUE(A2:B100) spills a de-duplicated copy into a new area without touching the source.

formulas.explanation: TRUE marks every value that appears more than once.
Microsoft 365 — returns a deduplicated spill range.

task: Split a full name into first and last columns
intro: A column of 'First Last' names splits cleanly with Text to Columns for a one-off job, or TEXTBEFORE/TEXTAFTER when you want live formulas that update with the data.

steps.heading: One-off: Text to Columns
steps.body: Select the column, go to Data → Text to Columns → Delimited → Space → Finish. Names land in two columns immediately.

steps.heading: Formulas: TEXTBEFORE / TEXTAFTER
steps.body: First name: =TEXTBEFORE(A1," "). Last name: =TEXTAFTER(A1," ",-1). Microsoft 365 only.

steps.heading: All versions: LEFT/MID + FIND
steps.body: First: =LEFT(A1,FIND(" ",A1)-1). Last: =MID(A1,FIND(" ",A1)+1,LEN(A1)).

formulas.explanation: First name in Microsoft 365.
Last name in any Excel version.

intro: Merging cells destroys your data layout — joining them with CONCAT, TEXTJOIN or the & operator keeps every value intact while producing the combined text you want.

steps.heading: TEXTJOIN for a list
steps.body: =TEXTJOIN(", ",TRUE,A1:C1) joins a range with a delimiter and skips empty cells.

steps.heading: CONCAT for a simple join
steps.body: =CONCAT(A1:C1) glues cells together with no separator.

steps.heading: The & operator for control
steps.body: =A1&" "&B1 gives you per-piece control over separators — ideal for 'First Last' with a single space.

formulas.explanation: Delimiter + skip-empty in one function.
Simplest option — no function needed.

intro: VLOOKUP accepts a single lookup value, so two-criteria lookups need either a helper key column or an INDEX+MATCH combo — XLOOKUP handles it natively in Microsoft 365.

steps.heading: Helper column
steps.body: Concatenate the criteria in a new column: =A2&"|"&B2. Then VLOOKUP that combined key: =VLOOKUP("East|Jan",C2:D10,2,FALSE).

steps.heading: No helper: INDEX + MATCH
steps.body: Use =INDEX(C2:C10,MATCH(1,(A2:A10="East")*(B2:B10="Jan"),0)). The multiplication acts as AND.

steps.heading: Microsoft 365: XLOOKUP
steps.body: =XLOOKUP(1,(A2:A10="East")*(B2:B10="Jan"),C2:C10) does the same thing without CSE or helpers.

formulas.explanation: Multi-criteria lookup without changing the data.
Microsoft 365 version — same logic, cleaner.

task: Count unique values in a column
intro: Counting distinct values takes a SUMPRODUCT/COUNTIF combo in classic Excel, or the purpose-built UNIQUE + COUNTA pair in Microsoft 365.

steps.heading: Microsoft 365: UNIQUE + COUNTA
steps.body: =COUNTA(UNIQUE(A2:A100)) returns the count of distinct non-blank values.

steps.heading: All versions: SUMPRODUCT
steps.body: =SUMPRODUCT(1/COUNTIF(A2:A100,A2:A100)) counts each distinct value once. Blanks break it — add a filter or IF inside COUNTIF if needed.

steps.heading: PivotTable alternative
steps.body: Insert → PivotTable, drag the column to Rows, and count the row labels — zero formulas.

formulas.explanation: Distinct count, Microsoft 365.
Distinct count in any version.

intro: Numbers stored as text refuse to sum and sort alphabetically. Excel flags them with green triangles — three quick fixes get them back to real numbers.

steps.heading: Error-checking menu
steps.body: Select the flagged cells, click the warning icon, and choose 'Convert to Number'. Fastest for small ranges.

steps.heading: Paste Special multiply
steps.body: Type 1 in a blank cell, copy it, select the text-numbers, then Paste Special → Multiply. Forces conversion in place.

steps.heading: VALUE or math coercion
steps.body: =VALUE(A1) converts one cell; multiplying by 1 (=A1*1) does the same inline inside larger formulas.

formulas.explanation: Purpose-built text→number converter.
Handles stray spaces and non-numeric cells gracefully.

task: Create a drop-down list in a cell
intro: Data Validation turns any cell into a drop-down — no code needed. A list source can be typed literals or a range, which keeps the menu in sync when the options change.

steps.heading: Open Data Validation
steps.body: Select the target cells, then Data → Data Validation → Allow: List.

steps.heading: Choose the source
steps.body: Type values separated by commas (Yes,No,Maybe) for a fixed list, or reference a range like =$E$2:$E$10 so the menu updates with the data.

steps.heading: Optional niceties
steps.body: Add an Input Message to explain the field, and an Error Alert to control whether invalid entries are rejected or just warned about.

formulas.explanation: Range source — the drop-down updates automatically when the list changes.

task: Lock a cell reference ($A$1 absolute reference)
intro: A plain reference like A1 drifts when you copy the formula down. Dollar signs lock it — and the F4 key cycles through all four reference styles while you edit.

steps.heading: Press F4 (or Cmd+T on Mac)
steps.body: While editing a formula, click inside a reference and press F4. Each press cycles: A1 → $A$1 → A$1 → $A1 → A1.

steps.heading: Know the four styles
steps.body: $A$1 locks column and row (fully absolute). A$1 locks only the row; $A1 locks only the column; A1 is fully relative.

steps.heading: Classic use case: rate lookup
steps.body: If a tax rate sits in E1, write =B2*$E$1 and fill down — every row multiplies by the same E1 instead of drifting to E2, E3…

formulas.explanation: Filling down keeps E1 fixed; B2 becomes B3, B4…

intro: There are two ways to show two decimals — formatting (display only) and ROUND (changes the value). Pick ROUND for money math; pick formatting for presentation.

steps.heading: ROUND in a formula
steps.body: =ROUND(A1,2) stores 19.476 as 19.48, so downstream sums match what you see.

steps.heading: Display-only: number format
steps.body: Select the cells → Ctrl+1 → Number → 2 decimal places. The underlying value stays 19.476.

steps.heading: TEXT for a string
steps.body: =TEXT(A1,"0.00") returns the text '19.48' — handy inside concatenated messages.

formulas.explanation: Changes the stored value.
Formats as text for use in strings.

task: Extract the domain from an email address
intro: The domain is everything after '@' — a MID + FIND pair in classic Excel, or a one-liner with TEXTAFTER in Microsoft 365.

steps.heading: Microsoft 365
steps.body: =TEXTAFTER(A1,"@") returns the domain in one call.

steps.heading: All versions
steps.body: =MID(A1,FIND("@",A1)+1,LEN(A1)) — FIND locates the @, MID takes everything after it.

steps.heading: Guard against bad input
steps.body: Wrap in IFERROR to return blank for cells that are not emails: =IFERROR(MID(A1,FIND("@",A1)+1,LEN(A1)),"").

formulas.explanation: Microsoft 365.
Every Excel version.

intro: COUNTIFS applies two tests to the same range — 'greater than 20 AND less than 60' — which is the simplest way to bucket values without a histogram.

steps.heading: Write the two criteria
steps.body: =COUNTIFS(A:A,">=20",A:A,"<=60") counts cells between 20 and 60 inclusive.

steps.heading: Use cell references for thresholds
steps.body: Concatenate the operator: =COUNTIFS(A:A,">="&D1,A:A,"<="&D2) so the bounds are editable in cells.

steps.heading: Same pattern for dates
steps.body: Criteria work on serial dates too — ">="&DATE(2026,1,1) filters a date column.

formulas.explanation: Inclusive between-count.
Bounds live in cells.

intro: LARGE ranks values without sorting, so summing the top 3, 5 or N is a single formula — no helper column, no sorting the source data.

steps.heading: Array constant
steps.body: =SUM(LARGE(A2:A20,{1,2,3})) adds the top 3 values.

steps.heading: N in a cell
steps.body: Put N in D1 and use =SUM(LARGE(A2:A20,ROW(INDIRECT("1:"&D1)))) for a controllable top-N total.

steps.heading: Microsoft 365: SORT + TAKE
steps.body: =SUM(TAKE(SORT(A2:A20,,-1),3)) sorts descending and sums the first 3.

formulas.explanation: Top-3 total in one formula.
Microsoft 365 variant.

intro: Imported data is full of stray spaces that break lookups and counts. TRIM collapses them in one call; SUBSTITUTE handles the non-breaking spaces TRIM misses.

steps.heading: TRIM the column
steps.body: In a helper column: =TRIM(A1) — removes leading/trailing spaces and squeezes inner doubles to one.

steps.heading: Catch non-breaking spaces
steps.body: Web-pasted data often uses CHAR(160). Use =TRIM(SUBSTITUTE(A1,CHAR(160)," ")) to clean both kinds.

steps.heading: Paste values back
steps.body: Copy the helper column, Paste Special → Values over the originals, then delete the helper.

formulas.explanation: Standard cleanup.
Also removes non-breaking spaces.

intro: Finding the holes in a dataset is a two-step job: Go To Special selects all blanks at once, or a COUNTA-based conditional format highlights them live as data changes.

steps.heading: Go To Special
steps.body: Select the range → Ctrl+G → Special → Blanks. Every empty cell is selected simultaneously — type =A1 and Ctrl+Enter to fill them all.

steps.heading: Conditional formatting
steps.body: Home → Conditional Formatting → 'Format only cells that contain' → Blanks → pick a fill colour.

steps.heading: Formula-driven highlight
steps.body: New Rule → 'Use a formula' → =LEN(TRIM(A1))=0 also catches cells that look filled but only contain spaces.

formulas.explanation: TRUE for blanks and space-only cells.
Compare against expected rows to gauge completeness.

task: Look up a price with VLOOKUP
intro: Use VLOOKUP when you have a table keyed by SKU, product, employee or region and need to return a value from the same row.

steps.heading: Put the lookup value in the first column
steps.body: VLOOKUP searches the first column of the selected range, so arrange or select the table that way.

steps.heading: Count the return column
steps.body: If the table starts at A and price is in B, the column index is 2.

steps.heading: Use exact match for IDs
steps.body: For SKUs and names, end with 0 or FALSE so Excel does not guess the closest row.

steps.heading: Handle missing matches
steps.body: If #N/A appears, check spelling, number formats and whether the value is actually in the first column.

formulas.explanation: Finds the value in D1 within A2:A4 and returns the matching price from B2:B4.
Shows a readable message instead of #N/A when the lookup fails.

task: Clean extra spaces in Excel text
intro: Imported names and labels often contain double spaces or leading/trailing blanks that break lookups. Clean the text before matching or reporting.

steps.heading: Trim the cell
steps.body: Use TRIM to remove leading and trailing spaces and collapse repeated internal spaces.

steps.heading: Standardize case
steps.body: Use UPPER or LOWER when the same label appears as "East", "east" and "EAST".

steps.heading: Clean before lookup
steps.body: Apply cleaning in a helper column first, then run VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP against the cleaned values.

formulas.explanation: Removes extra spaces from a text value.
Combines trimming and case normalization in one formula.

task: Calculate days between dates in Excel
intro: Excel stores dates as serial numbers, so date differences can be calculated with subtraction or the DAYS function.

steps.heading: Confirm the cells are dates
steps.body: If subtraction returns text or an error, format the cells as dates or rebuild them with DATE(year, month, day).

steps.heading: Use DAYS
steps.body: DAYS(end_date, start_date) returns the number of days between two dates in a clear order.

steps.heading: Extract year or month
steps.body: Use YEAR, MONTH or DAY when you need labels for reports rather than a day count.

formulas.explanation: Returns the number of days from the earlier date in A1 to the later date in A2.
Extracts the year from a date for grouping or labels.

task: Total sales for one region with SUMIF
intro: SUMIF totals only the rows that match a condition, which is faster than filtering a report by hand.

steps.heading: Select matching ranges
steps.body: The criteria range and sum range must cover the same rows, even if they are different columns.

steps.heading: Quote the criteria
steps.body: Use "East" for text or ">100" for numeric comparisons.

steps.heading: Add more conditions if needed
steps.body: Move to SUMIFS when you need region and month, or region and salesperson.

formulas.explanation: Adds B2:B4 only where A2:A4 equals "East".
Counts how many sales values are greater than 100.

intro: Freezing the top row keeps headers visible while you scroll through long sheets, which makes filtering, sorting and data entry much less error-prone.

steps.heading: Open the View tab
steps.body: On the ribbon, choose View → Freeze Panes. Excel offers Freeze Top Row, Freeze First Column and Freeze Panes.

steps.heading: Choose Freeze Top Row
steps.body: Select Freeze Top Row to lock row 1 in place. For a header in row 2, click any cell below the headers and use Freeze Panes instead.

steps.heading: Check the frozen line
steps.body: A thin gray line appears below the frozen rows. Scroll down to confirm the headers stay put.

steps.heading: Unfreeze when needed
steps.body: Return to View → Freeze Panes → Unfreeze Panes before changing the sheet layout.

intro: When row labels or IDs sit in column A, freezing the first column keeps them beside every record as you scroll right through wide tables.

steps.heading: Select column B
steps.body: Click the B column header, or select any cell in column B, so Excel knows where the freeze point should be.

steps.heading: Choose Freeze First Column
steps.body: Go to View → Freeze Panes → Freeze First Column.

steps.heading: For a custom freeze point
steps.body: If you also want the top row frozen, click the first data cell below and right of the headers — often B2 — then choose Freeze Panes.

steps.heading: Verify and unfreeze
steps.body: Scroll right; column A should remain visible. Use View → Freeze Panes → Unfreeze Panes to release it.

intro: Merging cells is best for titles and labels, not data tables — Excel keeps only the upper-left value and can break formulas that expect one value per cell.

steps.heading: Put text in the top-left cell
steps.body: Enter the title or label in the upper-left cell first; other values in the merged range will be discarded.

steps.heading: Select the cells
steps.body: Highlight the contiguous cells you want to combine, such as A1:D1 for a banner.

steps.heading: Choose a merge option
steps.body: Home → Alignment → Merge & Center dropdown offers Merge & Center, Merge Across, Merge Cells and Unmerge Cells.

steps.heading: Format the result
steps.body: Use Merge Across to center each row without merging columns into one cell, or Merge Cells when you do not want centering.

steps.heading: Unmerge carefully
steps.body: Unmerge Cells restores the grid but does not restore values that were discarded when the cells were merged.

intro: Paste Special → Transpose flips a vertical list into a horizontal row — or a two-dimensional range — without rewriting formulas by hand.

steps.heading: Copy the source range
steps.body: Select the cells you want to flip and press Ctrl+C.

steps.heading: Pick the destination
steps.body: Click the top-left cell where the transposed output should start, leaving enough empty space for the result.

steps.heading: Open Paste Special
steps.body: Home → Paste → Paste Special, or right-click the destination and choose Paste Special.

steps.heading: Check Transpose
steps.body: Tick Transpose and click OK. Values are rearranged while formulas are pasted as their current results.

intro: Blank rows split ranges, break charts and inflate pivot tables. Excel can select every blank cell in a range at once so you can delete the whole rows cleanly.

steps.heading: Select the range
steps.body: Click any cell in your data and press Ctrl+A, or drag to select exactly the rows you want to clean.

steps.heading: Find blanks with Go To Special
steps.body: Press Ctrl+G → Special → Blanks, or F5 → Special → Blanks, to select every empty cell in the range.

steps.heading: Delete entire rows
steps.body: Right-click one selected blank → Delete → Entire row → OK. Excel removes the rows, not just the selected cells.

steps.heading: Check for space-only cells
steps.body: Cells containing spaces are not truly blank. Clean them with TRIM first if Go To Special misses rows.

steps.heading: Alternative: filter blanks
steps.body: Add a helper column with =IF(COUNTA(A2:D2)=0,"Blank","Data"), filter to Blank, then delete the visible rows.

formulas.explanation: Flags rows where every cell in the range is empty.

intro: A PivotTable summarizes large ranges by dragging fields into Rows, Columns and Values, letting you total, count or average without writing formulas.

steps.heading: Prepare clean source data
steps.body: Use one header row, no blank rows inside the table, and consistent labels so the PivotTable groups correctly.

steps.heading: Insert the PivotTable
steps.body: Select any cell in the range, then Insert → PivotTable. Keep New Worksheet selected unless you need the summary beside the data.

steps.heading: Build the layout
steps.body: Drag fields to Rows and Columns for grouping, and drag a numeric field to Values for totals.

steps.heading: Change the calculation
steps.body: Open the field's value settings, such as Sum of Sales, to switch between Sum, Count, Average, Max or Min.

steps.heading: Refresh after edits
steps.body: Right-click the PivotTable → Refresh, or use PivotTable Analyze → Refresh All when source data changes.

intro: A bar or column chart turns rows of numbers into an instant visual comparison, and Excel's chart tools can relabel and restyle it without editing the data.

steps.heading: Select the data
steps.body: Highlight the category labels and values together, including headers so Excel can name the axes.

steps.heading: Insert the chart
steps.body: Insert → Charts → choose Clustered Column for vertical bars or Clustered Bar for horizontal bars.

steps.heading: Check the orientation
steps.body: If series and categories look swapped, Chart Design → Switch Row/Column fixes the layout.

steps.heading: Add labels and titles
steps.body: Use Chart Elements (+) for axis titles and data labels, then Chart Design to pick a style.

steps.heading: Format for readability
steps.body: Right-click an axis or bar to adjust bounds, gap width or colors; keep the message readable rather than decorative.

intro: Conditional formatting highlights patterns automatically — overdue dates, top performers, blanks and outliers update as the data changes.

steps.heading: Select the cells to format
steps.body: Highlight the data range, not the headers, before opening the rules.

steps.heading: Pick a preset
steps.body: Home → Conditional Formatting → Highlight Cells Rules for comparisons, or Top/Bottom Rules for ranks.

steps.heading: Try Color Scales or Data Bars
steps.body: Color Scales and Data Bars show magnitude across the range without picking a single threshold.

steps.heading: Use a formula for custom logic
steps.body: Choose New Rule → Use a formula → enter =B2>AVERAGE(B$2:B$10), then set the format. The formula is relative to the active cell.

steps.heading: Manage existing rules
steps.body: Conditional Formatting → Manage Rules lets you edit, reorder or delete rules that overlap.

formulas.explanation: Highlights cells above the range average; adjust the reference to match your active cell.

intro: Sorting by one column is easy; sorting by several columns at once keeps groups together — for example region first, then sales descending.

steps.heading: Start from any cell
steps.body: Click inside the table and use Data → Sort, not the A-Z buttons, so Excel detects headers and lists every column.

steps.heading: Add the first level
steps.body: In Sort, choose the primary column, order such as A to Z or Smallest to Largest, and keep My data has headers ticked if needed.

steps.heading: Add more levels
steps.body: Click Add Level for each tie-breaker, such as Region ascending then Sales descending.

steps.heading: Use Custom List for fixed order
steps.body: For months or weekdays, choose Custom List in Order and pick January…December or Sunday…Saturday.

steps.heading: Review blanks and totals
steps.body: Excel sorts blanks last by default. If the range includes totals, exclude them or sort only the data rows.

intro: Filtering hides rows that do not match criteria while leaving the worksheet intact, which is faster than copying data into a new report.

steps.heading: Turn on filters
steps.body: Select the table or range and click Data → Filter, or press Ctrl+Shift+L. Dropdown arrows appear in the header row.

steps.heading: Filter one column
steps.body: Click the arrow, untick Select All, then tick the values you want — or use Text Filters/Number Filters for conditions.

steps.heading: Combine columns
steps.body: Apply filters down several columns to narrow results, such as Region = East and Status = Open.

steps.heading: Clear or remove
steps.body: Filter → Clear removes criteria but keeps arrows; Data → Filter again removes the arrows entirely. Hidden rows are not deleted.

intro: Wrap Text keeps long labels readable inside a cell instead of spilling over neighbors or forcing a very wide column.

steps.heading: Select the cells
steps.body: Highlight the cells that contain long text, titles or descriptions.

steps.heading: Turn on Wrap Text
steps.body: Home → Alignment → Wrap Text. Excel increases row height automatically when the column width is fixed.

steps.heading: Add a manual line break
steps.body: Double-click the cell and press Alt+Enter where you want a new line inside the same cell.

steps.heading: Tune width and height
steps.body: Adjust column width and row height, or use Format → AutoFit Row Height after wrapping. Avoid wrapping inside formulas unless intentional.

intro: Autofit sizes columns to the widest visible content, which is faster than dragging boundaries when labels or numbers keep changing.

steps.heading: Select the columns
steps.body: Click one column header, drag across several, or press Ctrl+A to select the whole sheet.

steps.heading: Double-click the boundary
steps.body: Position the mouse on the line between two column letters until it becomes a double arrow, then double-click.

steps.heading: Or use the ribbon
steps.body: Home → Format → AutoFit Column Width applies the same fit to the selected columns. For rows, Home → Format → AutoFit Row Height.

steps.heading: Check the result
steps.body: Scroll through the sheet to confirm headers and values are not clipped; widen specific columns manually when autofit is too narrow for intentional spacing.

intro: Protecting a worksheet prevents accidental edits to formulas and layout while still letting users enter data in cells you explicitly unlock.

steps.heading: Unlock editable cells first
steps.body: Select the input cells, press Ctrl+1 → Protection, and untick Locked. Leave formula and label cells locked.

steps.heading: Review → Protect Sheet
steps.body: Go to Review → Protect Sheet. You can set a password, though it only prevents casual edits, not determined users.

steps.heading: Choose allowed actions
steps.body: In the dialog, tick what users may do — Select locked cells, Format cells, Insert rows — then click OK.

steps.heading: Test before sharing
steps.body: Try typing in a locked cell and an unlocked cell to confirm the protection behaves as intended.

steps.heading: Unprotect when needed
steps.body: Review → Unprotect Sheet removes protection. If a password was set, enter it first.

intro: Hiding rows and columns is useful for focusing a report or temporarily removing helper data without deleting it.

steps.heading: Select what to hide
steps.body: Click row numbers to hide rows or column letters to hide columns; Ctrl-click selects non-adjacent items.

steps.heading: Hide with the ribbon
steps.body: Home → Format → Hide & Unhide → Hide Rows or Hide Columns.

steps.heading: Use shortcuts
steps.body: Ctrl+9 hides selected rows and Ctrl+0 hides selected columns. Ctrl+Shift+9 and Ctrl+Shift+0 unhide them.

steps.heading: Show hidden data
steps.body: Select the rows or columns on both sides of the hidden area, then Home → Format → Hide & Unhide → Unhide Rows/Columns.

steps.heading: Remember it is not security
steps.body: Hidden rows still affect formulas and can be revealed. Use Protect Sheet if the data must stay private.

intro: Conditional formatting can spotlight repeated values instantly, while a COUNTIF helper column gives you a filterable list before you delete anything.

steps.heading: Highlight duplicates visually
steps.body: Select the range, then Home → Conditional Formatting → Highlight Cells Rules → Duplicate Values and choose a format.

steps.heading: Build a COUNTIF flag
steps.body: In a helper column enter =COUNTIF($A$2:$A$100,A2)>1 and fill down. TRUE marks values that appear more than once.

steps.heading: Filter to review
steps.body: Turn on Data → Filter and filter the helper column to TRUE to inspect only the duplicates.

steps.heading: Remove duplicates deliberately
steps.body: When ready, Data → Remove Duplicates can delete repeats, but copy the range first if the original must be preserved.

steps.heading: Check whole rows
steps.body: For duplicate rows across several columns, select all relevant columns in Remove Duplicates or use COUNTIFS with multiple criteria.

formulas.explanation: TRUE marks every value that appears more than once in the range.

intro: Percentages of total answer 'what share is this?' questions in budgets, surveys and scorecards — the key is dividing by the correct denominator.

steps.heading: Pick the denominator
steps.body: Use the grand total in one cell for share of total, or each row or column total for share within a group.

steps.heading: Write the division
steps.body: If B2 is the part and the total is in $B$101, enter =B2/$B$101 so the denominator stays fixed when copied.

steps.heading: Use SUM for a dynamic total
steps.body: =B2/SUM($B$2:$B$100) works when the total should recalculate from the range itself.

steps.heading: Format as percent
steps.body: Select the formula cells and press Ctrl+Shift+% or Home → Number Format → Percentage.

steps.heading: Check edge cases
steps.body: If totals can be zero, wrap the formula in IFERROR to avoid #DIV/0! errors.

formulas.explanation: Divides by a fixed total cell, useful when the denominator is already calculated.
Divides by a recalculated total for the whole range.
Returns 0 instead of #DIV/0! when the total is zero.

task: Convert a range to a table
intro: Excel Tables add filters, banded rows, calculated columns and structured references to a plain range with one shortcut.

steps.heading: Select the range
steps.body: Click any cell inside the data or select the full range including headers.

steps.heading: Insert the table
steps.body: Press Ctrl+T or Insert → Table. Confirm My table has headers is ticked, then click OK.

steps.heading: Use Table Design
steps.body: On the Table Design tab, rename the table, choose a style and turn Total Row on for quick totals.

steps.heading: Reference structured columns
steps.body: Formulas can use table names and column headers, such as =SUM(Sales[Amount]), instead of fragile cell ranges.

formulas.explanation: Structured references stay readable when rows are added or removed.

intro: Text to Columns turns one messy column into several clean columns using delimiters, fixed widths or dates — ideal for imports and pasted lists.

steps.heading: Select only the source column
steps.body: Highlight the column containing the combined text and leave room to the right for the output columns.

steps.heading: Start the wizard
steps.body: Data → Text to Columns opens a three-step wizard: Delimited, Fixed width or Date.

steps.heading: Choose delimiters
steps.body: For Delimited, tick the separator characters — comma, semicolon, tab, space or a custom character — and preview the split.

steps.heading: Set destination if needed
steps.body: On the final step, change Destination if the output should not start in the selected column, then click Finish.

steps.heading: Clean up after splitting
steps.body: Use TRIM on the new columns if extra spaces remain, and delete the original combined column only after checking the results.

intro: Excel interview questions usually test whether you can choose the right function, explain your logic and work quickly under time pressure.

steps.heading: Learn the core formula families
steps.body: Focus first on math functions such as SUM, COUNT and AVERAGE, then logic with IF, lookups with VLOOKUP or XLOOKUP, and conditional totals with SUMIF or COUNTIF.

steps.heading: Practice explaining your logic
steps.body: Interviewers often ask why a formula works, not just for the final answer. Be ready to explain ranges, exact match, criteria and absolute references.

steps.heading: Drill common question types
steps.body: Rehearse lookups, totals by condition, duplicate checks, text cleanup and simple date math. These map closely to spreadsheet exercises used in assessments.

steps.heading: Take a timed practice test
steps.body: Use the Practice page or Excel skills test guide to simulate exam conditions, then review every mistake until the formula feels automatic.

formulas.explanation: Classic interview lookup: find an exact value and return the matching result.
Shows that you understand conditional logic and text output.
Answers the common 'total by category' question efficiently.

intro: Employer Excel tests are usually timed, practical and focused on formulas, lookups, cleanup and shortcuts rather than theory.

steps.heading: Identify the test format
steps.body: Find out whether the assessment uses multiple choice, spreadsheet tasks or both. If possible, ask which Excel version and whether macros or pivot tables are included.

steps.heading: Build a formula checklist
steps.body: Make sure you can write SUM, COUNT, AVERAGE, IF, VLOOKUP or XLOOKUP, SUMIF, COUNTIF and basic text functions without hesitation.

steps.heading: Practice under time pressure
steps.body: Take short timed sessions on the Practice page. Track which question types slow you down, then repeat those exercises until they become routine.

steps.heading: Review common mistakes
steps.body: Check exact-match flags in lookups, absolute references in copied formulas, criteria syntax in SUMIF and whether dates are formatted as real dates.

formulas.explanation: A modern exact-match lookup with a readable default for missing values.
INDEX + MATCH is a reliable alternative when interviewers ask for lookup options.
Counts values meeting a numeric criterion, a frequent assessment task.

task: Practice for an Excel skills test
intro: A free Excel skills test should measure whether you can solve realistic spreadsheet tasks, not just recognize function names.

steps.heading: Start with a broad practice test
steps.body: Begin on the Practice page and complete a mixed set of formula, lookup, text, date and shortcut exercises.

steps.heading: Identify weak areas
steps.body: Note which prompts take too long or produce errors. Weak lookups, conditional totals and text cleanup are the most common gaps.

steps.heading: Repeat targeted drills
steps.body: Use the relevant lesson or function page to practice the exact skill, then return to the mixed test to confirm improvement.

steps.heading: Simulate the real test
steps.body: Set a timer, avoid opening reference notes, and work through questions in order. Review mistakes after the session rather than during it.

formulas.explanation: The baseline aggregate every skills test expects you to know.
A common formatting and accuracy check in assessments.
Text cleanup appears often because real spreadsheet data is messy.

task: Use Excel formulas in job interviews
intro: Job interviews often ask you to explain or recreate formulas for reporting, lookups, cleanup and conditional analysis.

steps.heading: Prepare lookup formulas
steps.body: Know when to use VLOOKUP, XLOOKUP and INDEX + MATCH, including exact match, approximate match and what to do when a value is missing.

steps.heading: Prepare conditional formulas
steps.body: Practice IF for logic checks, SUMIF or SUMIFS for totals by criteria, and COUNTIF or COUNTIFS for counts by criteria.

steps.heading: Prepare text and date formulas
steps.body: Be ready to clean imported data with TRIM, extract parts of text with LEFT, RIGHT, MID and FIND, and calculate date differences with DAYS or DATEDIF.

steps.heading: Explain the business answer
steps.body: After the formula, say what the result means in business terms: total sales by region, count of overdue invoices, or cleaned customer names.

formulas.explanation: Multiple criteria make conditional totals interview-ready.
Handles missing lookups gracefully, which is a common best-practice question.
Useful for date-difference questions in operations and finance roles.
